title: Terkîb-i Bend-i Nâ-Tamâm: an 'unfinished' terkib-i bend
greek: Arabic tarkīb 'composition'; Persian band 'tie, stanza'; nā-tamām 'incomplete'
short: A terkib-i bend, a poem of stanzas each closed by a different linking couplet; 'nâ-tamâm' (incomplete), presumably because only three stanzas exist.
body: In a terkîb-i bend each stanza (bend, hâne) is a run of couplets on one rhyme, closed by a linking couplet (vâsıta) with a new rhyme that changes from stanza to stanza; in the tercî-i bend the linking couplet repeats. Here there are three bends: on -em (âdem, elem, mâtem...), closed by 'Degil degil bu fenâ bezmi...'; on -ândır, closed by 'Yazık bu mertebe...'; and on -âh, closed by 'Gör añla...'. Uzun notes that terkib-i bends often have seven to nine couplets per stanza and that elegy is their chief subject; this one, like many, turns the elegiac mood on the world itself. 'Nâ-tamâm' (Persian nā-tamām) means 'incomplete', which suggests that the young poet left it unfinished.

sources.cite: Mustafa İsmet Uzun, 'Terciibend', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 40 (2011), pp. 487–489
Abdullah Uçman, 'Recâizâde Mahmud Ekrem', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 34 (2007), pp. 503–504
Haluk İpekten, Eski Türk Edebiyatı: Nazım Şekilleri ve Aruz (Istanbul: Dergâh), chapters on the bahirs

title: Nağme-i Seher and the young Ekrem
short: The poem belongs to Ekrem's first collection, Nağme-i Seher (1871), written in the old style before his turn to new poetry.
body: Uçman's article describes Nağme-i Seher as Ekrem's first verse collection, made up of poems in the old style; he worked in the Hariciye office among older poets of the divan tradition such as Leskofçalı Galib and Hersekli Ârif Hikmet and beside young reformers, and his new-style verse belongs to the later Zemzeme collections. The theme here, the misery and impermanence of the world, is the stock of hikemî (sententious) poetry, and the vocabulary is heavily Persian and Arabic: 'dâr-ı pür-mihen', 'this abode full of tribulations' (mihen is the Arabic plural of mihnet). Compare Ziya Paşa's gazel on the world as tavern and his Tercî-i Bend, written in the same decades.

sources.cite: Abdullah Uçman, 'Recâizâde Mahmud Ekrem', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 34 (2007), pp. 503–504

title: Metre: müctess (mefâilün feilâtün mefâilün feilün)
short: The lines scan mefâilün feilâtün mefâilün fa'lün, the müctess metre, very common in Ottoman lyric.
body: Line 5 scans cleanly: Bu ol-dı dey / de-ne-i rûz / gâ-rı bed-gir / dâr (. − . − / . . − − / . − . − / − −), that is mefâilün feilâtün mefâilün and a final fa'lün (the last foot may be feilün or fa'lün). This is the müctess-i müsemmen-i mahbûn, one of the commonest metres of the gazel. Some lines need the usual licences, for instance a short syllable held long ('pür-mi-he-ni' in l. 2). The scansion offered here is from the text; check it against a prosody handbook.

sources.cite: Haluk İpekten, Eski Türk Edebiyatı: Nazım Şekilleri ve Aruz (Istanbul: Dergâh), chapters on the bahirs

title: ayş u nûş: feasting and drinking
greek: Arabic ʿaysh 'living'; Persian nūsh 'drink, honey', nīsh 'sting'
short: What pleasure is there in feasting and drinking, if their end is the sting of calamity and the wound of pain?
body: 'Ayş' (Arabic ʿaysh, life, pleasant living) and 'nûş' (Persian nūsh, drinking; also sweetness, honey) form a fixed pair for revelry. The next line answers with its opposite: 'nîş-i belâ' (the sting of calamity; Persian nīsh, sting) and 'zahm-ı elem' (the wound of pain). The near-rhyme nûş / nîş, honey and sting, is a classical play (cinâs), since the bee gives both. The couplet states the theme of the whole first bend: every pleasure ends in mourning (mâtem, l. 6).

sources.cite: Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpaklı (eds and trans.), Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997), introduction and glossary

title: deydene: the habit of an ill-natured age
greek: Arabic daydan 'custom'; Persian rōzgār 'time, fortune'; bad-kirdār 'evil-doing'
short: This is the custom of malicious fortune: every joy ends in mourning.
body: 'Deydene' (Arabic daydan) is habit or custom; 'rûzgâr' (Persian rōzgār) means time, the age, fortune (in modern Turkish it means 'wind'); 'bed-girdâr' (Persian bad-kirdār) is 'evil in conduct'. Time is personified as a wicked actor whose fixed habit is to turn every pleasure (meserret, Arabic masarra) into mourning (mâtem). The personification of time and the heavens as hostile agents is the base of the classical complaint of fortune (şikâyet-i felek).

sources.cite: Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpaklı (eds and trans.), Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997), introduction and glossary
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'felek'

title: çerh-i felek: the turning wheel of heaven
short: Does the wheel of heaven always turn as we wish? One day its revolution demands the opposite.
body: 'Çerh' (Persian charkh, wheel) and 'felek' (Arabic falak, celestial sphere) together name the revolving heavens of Ptolemaic cosmology, believed to govern fortune. The image is close to the European Wheel of Fortune. 'İktizâ-yı devr' is 'what the rotation requires'. The archive's 'devr-i dijem' at the end of l. 10 is obscure and may be a transcription error for a word rhyming in -em; the sense of the line, that the wheel's turning eventually reverses every wish, is clear.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'felek'
Walter G. Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song: Ottoman Lyric Poetry (Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1985)

anchor: Gerek gedâ-yı muhakkar gerek şeh-i efham
title: Beggar and king
short: No one in the world gets what he desires, neither the despised beggar nor the greatest king.
body: 'Gedâ' (Persian gadā) is a beggar, 'muhakkar' (Arabic muḥaqqar) despised; 'şeh' is the shah, and 'efham' (Arabic afkham) the most magnificent. The pairing of beggar and king is the great levelling commonplace of moral verse: fortune and death make no distinction. Ziya Paşa's tesdis in this archive uses the same contrast ('Be he Khusrev ... or be he beggar'), and the thought goes back to the Persian moralists, for whom the grave equalises shah and dervish alike.

sources.cite: Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpaklı (eds and trans.), Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997), introduction and glossary

title: kabz u bast: contraction and expansion
short: Does the wise man pay any heed to the world's contractions and expansions, its tightening and loosening of the heart?
body: 'Kabz' (Arabic qabḍ, contraction, seizing) and 'bast' (Arabic basṭ, expansion) are technical terms of Sufism for the alternating states of the heart: depression and joy, God withholding and God granting. The Qur'an says that God 'withholds and gives abundance' (Qur'an 2:245, yaqbiḍu wa-yabsuṭu). The 'ârif', the gnostic who knows God, gives them no 'existence' (vücûd), that is, he does not let them rule him. The poet applies the mystic's vocabulary to the ups and downs of worldly fortune (dehr).

sources.cite: Qur'an 2:245
Victoria Rowe Holbrook, The Unreadable Shores of Love: Turkish Modernity and Mystic Romance (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1994)

title: Being turns out to be non-being
short: If the world is imagined as it really is, its existence proves non-existence, its pleasure and grace turn to pain and grief.
body: 'Vücûd' and 'adem' (Arabic wujūd and ʿadam) are being and non-being, terms of Islamic philosophy and Sufi metaphysics. For the Sufi, only God truly exists and the world is a shadow; for the moralist, the world's goods are illusory. The next bend opens with the same idea: in this world 'its non-being and its being are all one' (yogu vârı cümle yeksândır, l. 19), and the one who knows this secret laughs at the state of the world.

sources.cite: Victoria Rowe Holbrook, The Unreadable Shores of Love: Turkish Modernity and Mystic Romance (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1994)

title: The first linking couplet (vâsıta)
greek: Persian bazm 'feast'; Arabic fanāʾ 'passing away'; ghurūr 'delusion, pride'
short: 'No, no: this feast of mortality is not a place of peace; beware lest the cup of pride ruin your heart.'
body: The vâsıta closes the first bend on a new rhyme (huzûr / gurûr). 'Bezm' (Persian bazm) is a drinking party, the classic setting of the gazel; 'fenâ' (Arabic fanāʾ) is mortality, passing away. The world is a banquet where nobody may stay, and 'câm-ı gurûr', the cup of pride (or of delusion: gurûr means both), is the dangerous drink served there. In a terkib-i bend the linking couplets carry the moral; here each states the lesson of its stanza.

sources.cite: Mustafa İsmet Uzun, 'Terciibend', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 40 (2011), pp. 487–489
Walter G. Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song: Ottoman Lyric Poetry (Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1985)

title: The rose that is a thorn
short: This garden of passing things is a strange rose-garden of pains, whose open rose is in the same state as the desert thorn.
body: 'Mugaylân' (Arabic umm ghaylān, the acacia of the Arabian desert, with long thorns) is the thorn bush of the wilderness where the lover Mecnun wanders. The rose-garden (gülşen) and rose (gül), the most cherished images of Ottoman lyric, are equated with it: in this world the opened rose (gül-i şüküfte) is no better than a thorn. The figure reverses the usual hope of the garden image (the beloved, spring, union) to say that every beauty is already pain.

sources.cite: Walter G. Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song: Ottoman Lyric Poetry (Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1985)
Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpaklı (eds and trans.), Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997), introduction and glossary

title: kevn ü fesâd: generation and corruption
greek: Arabic kawn wa-fasād 'generation and corruption' (Aristotle, Peri geneseōs kai phthoras)
short: If the order of coming-to-be and passing-away seems impossible, do not wonder: the world's foundation has been in disorder since it began.
body: 'Kevn ü fesâd' (Arabic kawn wa-fasād) translates the title of Aristotle's treatise On Generation and Corruption, and in Islamic philosophy names the sublunary world where things come into being and decay. The poet uses the philosopher's term to say that disorder (perîşânlık) is built into the world from the start. Philosophical vocabulary in a moral poem is typical of the learned divan manner Ekrem inherited.

sources.cite: Haluk İpekten, Eski Türk Edebiyatı: Nazım Şekilleri ve Aruz (Istanbul: Dergâh), chapters on the bahirs
Victoria Rowe Holbrook, The Unreadable Shores of Love: Turkish Modernity and Mystic Romance (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1994)

title: Second linking couplet: the fool who laughs
short: Pity the base man of sick judgement whose words make even a madman laugh.
body: 'Sakîm' (Arabic saqīm) is sick, 'dûn' base or low; 'hande-bahş' (Persian khanda-bakhsh) is 'laughter-giving'. The madman (merd-i mecnûn) is ordinarily the butt of laughter; here the man who trusts the world is so foolish that the madman laughs at him. The image picks up the earlier line in which the one who knows the world's secret is 'handân', laughing (l. 20). The vâsıta again distils the stanza's argument.

title: The mirage taken for water
short: You take the mirage for water and fantasy for real; one day this will throw you into a pit.
body: The archive's 'sınırsın' is evidently 'sanırsın', you suppose. The mirage (serâb, Persian sarāb) taken for water recalls the Qur'anic simile for the deeds of unbelievers, 'like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty man thinks is water' (Qur'an 24:39). 'Fütâde-i çâh' (fallen into a well, Persian uftāda) may also evoke Joseph thrown into the well, though the main sense is simply ruin. The desert (bâdiye) that leads its travellers astray (l. 38) is the world itself.

sources.cite: Qur'an 24:39
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'serap'

title: Refuge at God's threshold
greek: Persian dargāh 'court, threshold'; panāh 'refuge'; Arabic ṣunʿ 'workmanship'
short: The third bend turns from complaint to counsel: in every hard task take refuge at God's court, and rub your forehead in praise on His threshold.
body: 'Dergâh' (Persian dargāh) is a royal court or threshold, and also a dervish lodge; 'penâh' (Persian panāh) is refuge. The poem now moves from the vanity of the world to trust in God (tevekkül): the cry 'yâ Allâh' opens the lock (kufl) of the treasury of graces; without God's help our only work would be a wail of 'alas' (tazallüm-i vâh). 'Cebîn-i hamdi ... sûde-i dergâh' means 'rub the forehead of praise on the threshold', the gesture of prostration. The final linking couplet tells the reader to contemplate God's art (sun') and not to impose meaning on the world with a short reason (akl-ı kasîr).

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'dergâh'
